summary: A glossary of terms specific to the Internet, written to help users understand the language they come across. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A dictionary of Internet words, to help newcomers understand what everyone is talking about.

subtitle: An alphabetical glossary of Internet-specific terms, written to help ordinary users follow the language.

tldr.problem: Newcomers meet a flood of jargon and acronyms when they start using the Internet, and general networking glossaries do not focus on Internet-specific terms.
tldr.mechanism: The memo is an alphabetical glossary, from non-letter entries and 10Base2 through Z. Entries define terms, cross-reference each other with See and See also, and often credit a source.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, FYI 18, that obsoletes RFC 1392. Its definitions reflect August 1996 and many have since changed.

today: RFC 1983 is an Informational memo from August 1996 that obsoletes RFC 1392. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, but it is a snapshot of terminology from 1996.

sections.title: Purpose of the Glossary
sections.content:
RFC 1983 is FYI 18, edited by G. Malkin. The abstract notes that many networking glossaries exist and that this one concentrates on terms specific to the Internet. It still includes entries for some basic terms and acronyms because other entries refer to them.

It is the work of the User Glossary Working Group of the User Services Area of the Internet Engineering Task Force. It obsoletes RFC 1392, the previous version.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a word list for the Internet, made by a group who wanted newcomers to feel less lost.

sections.title: How Entries Are Organized
sections.content:
The glossary is ordered alphabetically, with a table of contents that lists each letter and the page it starts on, beginning with non-letter entries such as 10Base2, 802.x and the smiley :-).

An entry gives a definition, then may add See also: pointers to related terms. An entry that is only an alias reads See: followed by the main term, as with ACK pointing to Acknowledgment. Many definitions end with a tag such as [Source: ZEN] or [Source: RFC1208], which names an item in the References list at the end.
sections.plainLanguage: Like a dictionary, it is in ABC order. Some words just say to look at another word, and many show where the definition came from.

sections.title: A Sample of the Entries
sections.content:
The entries run from hardware to social conventions. The four 10Base entries describe 10Mbps baseband physical layers. Others define protocols such as ARP, services such as anonymous FTP, and organizations such as the IETF, which the glossary describes as a large, open community of network designers, operators, vendors, and researchers.

Some entries describe the RFC series itself. The glossary defines Request For Comments (RFC) as the document series begun in 1969 that describes the Internet suite of protocols and related experiments, and notes that very few RFCs describe Internet standards, though all Internet standards are written up as RFCs. It defines an FYI as a subseries of RFCs that are not technical standards or protocol descriptions. For the DNS entry it lists the main top-level domains such as .COM, .EDU, .GOV and .MIL.
sections.plainLanguage: The words in it range from cables to etiquette, for example what the Internet's big club of engineers is called and what a smiley face means.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that security is not explicitly discussed in the document, but that some of the glossary's entries are security related. It points readers to entries such as Access Control List (ACL), authentication, Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT), cracker, encryption, Kerberos, Pretty Good Privacy (PGP), Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM), RSA, Trojan Horse, virus and worm.
sections.plainLanguage: The book is not about safety, but it does explain many safety words, like virus and encryption.
